The hover double‑outline/glow on small icon‑style buttons was caused by overlapping CSS box‑shadows—one from the component hover token and another from an outer focus ring variable—that produced stacked shadows. [1]

Redwood proposed per‑tenant deterministic pseudonymization: each tenant receives a unique KMS‑wrapped salt, and trace/request IDs are hashed with HMAC‑SHA256 + salt then truncated to 16 bytes (base64) for storage. [1]  
This approach preserves correlation of IDs within a tenant’s account while preventing cross‑tenant correlation by Redwood, and the keys can be customer‑managed (BYOK) if required. [1]

The proposed change is to implement a stepped batching policy in the serving runtime. [1]  
This policy lets the scheduler be configured with an ordered list of candidate batch sizes (e.g., [1][2]) and per‑step latency bounds. [1]

The mismatch occurs because the Suggestions estimator assumes full (100%) adoption and a compute‑cost basis, while the customer’s billing reflects net invoiced totals after discounts/credits, partial rollout, cache‑warm‑up effects, and time‑window differences; the UI does not surface these assumptions clearly.  

- Estimator assumes full enablement for the shown scope and does not automatically adjust for partial rollout percentages unless telemetry provides a separate variant. [1]  
- It uses a trailing‑7‑day baseline and compute‑cost attribution (GPU‑sec + token pricing) and excludes invoice‑only items such as platform fees, support add‑ons, taxes, and credits/commit discounts. [1] [1] [1]  
- Cache warm‑up can lower realized savings in the first 6–12 hours after enablement, while the estimator assumes steady‑state uplift. [1] [1]  
- Time‑window mismatch: the estimator’s stale_as_of period (trailing 7 days) may not align with the customer’s local‑time billing days or UTC invoice periods. [1] [1] [1]  
- UI labels the figure as “Estimated savings” without prominently noting the assumptions (full adoption, compute‑cost basis); the detail is buried in the drawer’s “Assumptions” section. [1] [2]  
- Because the list is sortable by $/day, users often treat the number as realized savings. [1]  

To prevent this confusion, the following UI and estimator changes are recommended:  

- Make the assumptions explicit in the UI, e.g., add an inline callout: “Assumes 100% of traffic” and “Compute‑cost estimate (not invoice total)”. [1] [1]  
- Provide a way to scale the estimate by the actual rollout percentage (e.g., an optional “adoption_factor” field or UI control) so the displayed savings reflect partial deployment. [1] [1]  
- Align the comparison window by defaulting to UTC and to the estimator’s stale_as_of period, and advise customers to use Console Usage Analytics “Inference cost (compute)” rather than invoice totals for apples‑to‑apples checks. [1] [1]  
- Add guidance to evaluate over at least 48–72 hours after enablement to account for cache warm‑up and to look at cache‑hit metrics alongside compute cost. [1] [1]  
- Improve documentation and a reconciliation section that explains compute‑cost vs invoice totals, the impact of credits/commit discounts, and how to map the delta. [1] [1]  
- Consider surfacing the price source (effective vs list price) and flagging when a fallback price is used, so users know if the dollar estimate is based on list pricing. [2] [2]

[1]  
According to the region‑degradation scenario, once the incident is confirmed, open a status page incident within 10 minutes of confirmation. [2]  
Customer update cadence: during active mitigation target 30–60 minutes depending on severity; once stable, provide hourly updates. [3] [3]  
Credits wording: avoid labeling the event as an “SLA breach” unless the contract calculation is completed; instead state that we experienced a service degradation impacting streaming stability in us‑east and that we are reviewing the request under our service credit policy, and if a goodwill credit is decided, label it as goodwill, not as an SLA admission. [3]

The standardized telemetry header is "x-redwood-template-tags", carrying semicolon‑separated "k=v" pairs with keys limited to an allow‑list and each value ≤64 characters. [1]  
Templates can disable this header via the environment variable REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=off when a corporate proxy blocks it. [1]  
The product decision is to make template‑origin telemetry tagging opt‑in, so default quickstart templates do NOT send the telemetry header unless explicitly enabled. [2] [2]  
Therefore, when a corporate proxy blocks the telemetry header, the default (header‑off) behavior lets requests succeed; if a user opts in and the header is blocked, the request will be rejected until the header is disabled or allowlisted. [2] [2] [2]

[3]

Per the region‑pinning policy, the following request/response data are considered “customer content” that must remain in‑region for residency‑strict traffic:

- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by the customer  [2]

After the org signing‑key rotation on 2026-03-09, some release runners retained an outdated keyring that still trusted the old key fingerprint while the artifacts were signed with the new key, and the keysync service truncated the new public‑key export because the keyserver returned a chunked‑transfer encoding, producing a malformed pubkey blob that caused GPG to report BAD_SIGNATURE. [1] [1]  
Immediate operational mitigations: Ops added the previous GPG public key to a temporary allowlist on three prod runners (release‑runner‑prod‑03/04/07), which allowed those runners to verify the hotfix candidate; they also ran a force‑import job to refresh the keyring on those runners, verifying pipeline success; and they temporarily rolled back the signing host to the previous key to unblock hotfix promotions while a permanent fix was prepared. [1] [1]

The migration is stuck because another Postgres session holds the advisory lock required by the migration job, causing a lock timeout and the UI to remain on “Running migrations”. [1]  
Support’s guided fix is to identify the blocking backend with a query on `pg_stat_activity` (e.g., `SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start AS xact_age, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY xact_age DESC;`) and terminate it via `pg_terminate_backend(<pid>)`, then re‑run the migration job (delete the failed pod and re‑apply the hook or use `helm upgrade --reuse-values`). [1]  
Before attempting a retry or rollback, collect: installer logs bundle (installer.log, migration runner output, timestamps for upgrade start and when it appeared stuck); cluster events around the installer/job pod (`kubectl get pods -n redwood-private`, `kubectl describe pod <installer/migrations pod>`, `kubectl logs <installer/migrations pod> --since=2h`); control‑plane version details (current version prior to upgrade, target version, installer version); Postgres connectivity and health (confirmation Postgres is reachable from the cluster network, any recent DB maintenance); and a DB lock snapshot (output of `pg_stat_activity` or a similar lock‑wait query). [2] [2] [2]

The duplicate tool/webhook executions during streaming chat retries were caused by a mismatch in Unicode normalization of idempotency keys—SDKs sent keys in different normalizations (Python NFD, Go NFC) while the edge proxy performed header folding/percent-encoding on HTTP/2, resulting in different byte sequences for keys containing non‑ASCII characters. [1] [1]
The issue occurred only when the idempotency key contained composed Unicode (e.g., emoji/diacritics) and the request traversed HTTP/2 through the edge proxy. [1] [1]
As a short‑term workaround, customers were advised to base64‑encode the idempotency key before sending it, which eliminated the duplicates. [1] [1]
The server‑side fix was to canonicalize incoming idempotency keys to UTF‑8 NFC on ingestion and make the lookup normalization‑tolerant, with the patch (serving‑runtime PR #1220) merged to main and scheduled for staging on 2026‑03‑15 and production on 2026‑03‑18. [1] [1] [1]
At temp=0.0 with strict JSON + canonicalization, price-normalization correctness is ~96%, up from an earlier ~89% without canonicalization. [1]

The emergency rollback procedure for a Serving Runtime release (Hosted and Dedicated) begins by pausing any in‑flight rollout or progressive rollout controller.  [1] [1]  
Next, the current runtime release identifier, intended rollback target, blast radius, primary symptom, and confirmation that the prior release is known‑good are recorded in the incident channel.  [1]  

**Hosted rollback** – the Hosted runtime is pinned to the rollback target (e.g., `rw-release set-tag …`), then regions are redeployed in the order non‑critical region → remaining canary cohort → all regions currently on the bad release; after each region completes, verification checks that the 5xx rate normalizes, GPU utilization returns to expected levels, and TTFT and token/s recover to baseline.  [2] [2] [1] [1]  

**Dedicated rollback** – impacted Dedicated clusters/tenants are identified via the “Dedicated / Runtime Release Adoption” dashboard, each tenant is confirmed to be on the bad release, the pipeline rollback procedure is executed per cluster, and for high‑sensitivity tenants coordination with CS for outbound communications and approvals is performed.  [2] [1]  

The rollback target tag is then locked to prevent auto‑advance (e.g., `rw-release lock …`).  [2]  

**Post‑rollback validation** – the incident remains open until metrics are stable for 30 minutes (Hosted) or 60 minutes (Dedicated), request latency distributions are confirmed to have returned to baseline with no new error modes, and autoscaling is observed to stabilize (watching for over‑provisioning due to the regression).  [1] [1] [1]  

Throughout the process, SRE monitors fleet‑level SLOs and regional health signals (request_error_rate, ttft_p95_ms, tokens_per_sec, gpu_oom_count) using the Hosted Inference / Runtime Release Health dashboard.  [1] [1] [1]

Redwood Inference’s end‑to‑end process for rotating production secrets (including emergency rotation) consists of the following steps:

- Identify the secret name/path and all consumers (see the Credential Dependencies inventory) and confirm whether the rotation is planned or emergency  [1]  
- Ensure appropriate access (normal approvals for planned rotations or break‑glass access for emergencies)  [1]  
- For planned rotations, prefer the dual‑valid window when downstream systems can accept two credentials temporarily; otherwise use a cutover  [1]  
- For emergency rotations, declare the incident in the channel, list candidate secrets, link any break‑glass event, and enable audit logging  [2] [2]  
- Determine rotation order: Tier 0 secrets (signing keys, privileged service tokens) first, then Tier 1 secrets (database credentials, message‑bus credentials, third‑party keys with broad scopes)  [2] [1]  
- For each secret: confirm its consumers from the Credential Dependencies inventory, choose the rotation pattern (dual‑valid if available, otherwise cutover), rotate the issuer‑side credential, update the Vault or secret store, and restart/redeploy consumers as required  [2] [1]  
- Validate per‑service health (auth failures, latency, error rate); if failures persist beyond 10 minutes and customer impact is increasing, pause and reassess (rollback vs continue)  [2] [1]  
- Record exact timestamps for the issuer‑side change and each consumer rollout  [2] [1]  
- After containment, enumerate all downstream consumers and rotate any derived tokens  [1]  
- Documentation: planned rotations require a change record with impacted services, steps, and validation; emergency rotations are documented in the incident timeline followed by a post‑mortem action list  [1] [2]  
- Ownership: the secret owner is the owning service team; Security sets minimum standards and reviews exceptions  [3] [3]

Northwind Analytics reported timeouts when using JSON‑schema structured output on the hosted API. [1]  
They observed intermittent client‑side 60‑second timeouts with large schemas containing dozens of properties, nested arrays, and anyOf/oneOf sections. [2] [3]  
Their specific request IDs (req_1f3b8c0c, req_6aa2d19e, req_09a3f7d1) were correlated to the timeouts. [4] [4]  
Suggested mitigations included reducing max_output_tokens and simplifying the schema (avoiding large anyOf/oneOf). [4] [4]

The process begins with preconditions: emergency change approvals must be recorded per the emergency‑change policy, an incident channel (or Slack thread) with an identified Incident Commander must exist, and a rollback plan (previous runtime image tag + restart procedure) must be in place  [1]. All emergency changes require two‑person approval before production impact: the Incident Commander (or on‑call SRE if not in incident mode) and the Service Owner (or delegate) for the component being changed  [2]; additional approvals are added based on scenario (Security on‑call for security‑related exploits, Product on‑call or responsible PM for customer‑visible behavior changes, and Customer Success escalation manager for any change requiring customer maintenance coordination such as Dedicated/Private)  [2]. For Dedicated hotfixes specifically, approval also includes Dedicated service owner sign‑off and Customer Success escalation manager sign‑off on customer messaging  [3] [3].

Next, a hotfix branch is cut: branch naming follows hotfix/runtime‑<YYYYMMDD>-<short‑issue>, only the minimum fix commit(s) are cherry‑picked, and a CHANGELOG entry under “Runtime Hotfixes” is added  [1].

The build and signing step requires that the PR be approved per emergency policy, the label hotfix-ready be added, and the “Release Runtime Hotfix” workflow (GitHub Actions release-hotfix.yml or internal Buildkite runtime-hotfix-build when GitHub Actions is degraded) be triggered with inputs base image tag (previous production runtime) and new tag suffix (e.g., hotfix‑2026-02-02a)  [4] [4]. Artifacts produced are the signed container image ghcr.io/redwoodinference/runtime:<tag>, an SBOM uploaded to s3://redwood-release-artifacts/sbom/runtime/<tag>.json, and a provenance attestation to s3://redwood-release-artifacts/provenance/runtime/<tag>.intoto  [4] [4]. Before rollout, signatures must be verified with cosign verify and cosign verify-attestation for SLSA provenance; exceptions are rare and require Security on‑call approval, with only a temporary SBOM upload delay allowed if the SBOM is generated and attached to the incident within 4 hours—image signing cannot be skipped  [4].

For Dedicated clusters, the rollout owner must gather required inputs: customer name + cluster ID, current runtime image tag, target runtime image tag, impact statement (expected restart behavior), rollback image tag, and whether the issue is customer‑specific or global  [3] [3]. Required approvals for the Dedicated rollout are IC or SRE on‑call approval, Dedicated service owner approval, and Customer Success escalation manager sign‑off on customer messaging  [3] [3] [2].

Customer communications must be reviewed by the Customer Success owner for the account and the Product Manager for inference; for Private customers in regulated environments, a Security review is also required  [5]. Templates include subject‑line options and mandatory opt‑out language (offering to pin the previous model version for at least 30 days)  [5]. The rollout plan must link to the customer ticket(s) and note when the communication was sent  [5]. If a hotfix rollout is planned, the rollout window and rollback criteria must be provided in customer‑friendly terms  [6]; Sev‑1 status‑page templates (initial investigation, update, and resolution messages) are also used  [6].

The rollout executes as follows: first, a canary is deployed to one Dedicated cluster (preferring an internal dogfood dedicated cluster or the lowest‑traffic customer, with CSEM approval)  [3] [3]. The canary is validated for 30 minutes, checking success rate, p95 latency, GPU OOM, restart frequency, and customer‑specific health checks  [3] [3]. Remaining impacted clusters are then scheduled, with no more than 3 clusters rolled in parallel unless the IC approves additional parallelism  [3] [3]. (Hosted environments follow the same canary/validation approach via the progressive rollout controller referenced in the rollback procedure  [7].)

If a rollback is needed, the emergency rollback procedure is: pause the progressive rollout controller, pin the runtime release tag to the rollback target, trigger redeploy, verify health and metrics, and document the outcome in the incident/change record  [7].

All steps—from approvals through build, signing, rollout, communication, and possible rollback—constitute Redwood Inference’s complete end‑to‑end process for shipping an emergency serving‑runtime hotfix to both Hosted and Dedicated production environments.
